questions.learningObjective: explain how to build an equation for a bill with two rates
questions.stem: The software team's ticket bills 40 dollars per hour for 2 hours of setup plus 90 dollars per hour for the remaining hours. Explain how to build an equation that models this bill.

answer.exemplar: Start by naming what is unknown, for example the total cost C for h hours of work. The first 2 hours are billed at 40 dollars, contributing 2 times 40, and every hour after that is billed at 90 dollars, contributing 90(h - 2). The model is therefore C = 2(40) + 90(h - 2). Splitting the hours matters because the two groups carry different rates, and a single blended rate would misprice the setup block. A good check is to plug in h = 2 and confirm that the formula gives exactly the 80 dollars the setup block costs.

questions.explanation: Naming the unknown first keeps the equation readable, and splitting the hours shows the two groups carry different rates. A single blended rate would hide where one price ends.

answer.exemplar: A rate of change compares two amounts by dividing the change in the measured quantity by the change in the input. Here the load rose by 85 minus 40, which is 45 percentage points, over 3 hours, so the rate is 15 percentage points each hour. That number is a rate, not a total, and it says nothing about what happens outside the interval from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. unless the team has reason to believe the pattern continues. The team can use the rate to plan capacity during the busy stretch, but it should measure again later rather than assume the same rate holds all day.

questions.explanation: The load rose 45 percentage points over 3 hours, so the rate of change is 15 percentage points each hour. A rate describes the pattern between two readings and does not predict later ones.
questions.hint: Change in output divided by change in input.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Meaning of the constant of proportionality
questions.learningObjective: explain which part of a cost rule is the constant of proportionality
questions.stem: A software team's ticket gives a cost rule of 12 dollars per record plus a 5 dollar processing fee. Explain what the constant of proportionality is in this rule and what it is not.

answer.exemplar: The rule cost equals 12n plus 5, so the constant of proportionality is 12, the number of dollars charged for each record. A constant of proportionality is the rate that scales with the input, so it says how output changes as the input grows, and 12n grows exactly in step with n. The 5 dollar processing fee is not part of it, because that fee is charged once and does not change when more records are processed, which is why it belongs in the added term rather than inside the rate. One way to test this is to compare two totals: the difference between them is 12 times the difference in records, and nothing about the fee appears in that difference.

questions.explanation: The constant of proportionality is 12, the part that scales with the number of records. The 5 dollar fee is charged once and does not change as records are added, so it is not part of a rate.
questions.hint: The rate is the part that changes when the input changes.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Inverse variation
questions.learningObjective: explain how time changes when processors increase on a fixed workload
questions.stem: A software team's ticket tracks a fixed workload that takes 240 processor-minutes in total. Explain how the time changes as the number of processors increases.

answer.exemplar: The workload is a fixed amount of work, so the time and the number of processors must satisfy a constant product. With one processor the job takes 240 minutes, so the product is 240, and with p processors the time is 240 over p minutes. This is inverse variation: doubling the processors halves the time, and no processor count can make the time zero. The model also breaks down for very large p, because real overhead makes the last few processors worth less than a perfect share. Even so, within a reasonable range the rule is a good planning tool for deciding how many machines to request.

questions.explanation: The total work stays at 240 processor-minutes, so more processors means less time and the product stays fixed. Halving the time when the processor count doubles is the pattern of inverse variation.
questions.hint: The work is fixed, so time and processors trade off.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Extending a model past the data
questions.learningObjective: explain what a linear model can and cannot claim beyond the data
questions.stem: A software team's ticket reports that a server used 200 GB of storage in week one and 260 GB in week two. Explain what a linear model can and cannot tell the team about week six.

answer.exemplar: Fitting a line to the two measured points gives 60 GB per week of growth, so the model predicts 200 + 60(6 - 1) = 500 GB in week six. That number is an extrapolation: it continues a pattern the team observed over a very short span, and nothing in the two readings rules out a slowdown, a cleanup, or a sudden jump. So the model is useful for planning and for spotting trends, but the team should check it against later measurements rather than treat 500 GB as a fact. A good habit is to rewrite the estimate as a range and to note how many weeks of data the range assumes.

questions.explanation: The line through the two points rises by 60 GB a week, so it points to about 500 GB in week six. Extending a line past the data gives a reasonable guess, not a guarantee, because the pattern may not hold.
questions.hint: Extend the line, but call the result an estimate.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Answer ruled out by the context
questions.learningObjective: explain how to decide between two algebraic answers using the situation
questions.stem: A software team's ticket produces the roots 6 and negative 3 after solving a quadratic. Explain how to decide which root answers the ticket's question.

answer.exemplar: An algebraic solution is only a candidate until the situation is checked. In the ticket the variable measures a length of time, and time cannot be negative, so the root 6 survives and negative 3 is discarded. The test is not whether the algebra was done correctly but whether the value means something in the problem: a number of servers must be a whole number, a percentage must lie between 0 and 100, and a time must be positive. Recording why a root was rejected is part of the solution, because a reader needs to know the value was tested rather than overlooked.

questions.explanation: A root is only a candidate until the situation is tested, and a negative time is not a real duration. The check is about meaning, not about whether the algebra was done correctly.
questions.hint: Ask whether the value means something in the situation.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Distance where two plans cost the same
questions.learningObjective: explain the meaning of a break-even point for a cost comparison
questions.stem: A software team's ticket compares a monthly hosting plan with a yearly plan. Explain what a break-even point means and why the team should look for one.

answer.exemplar: A break-even point is the input where two cost rules give exactly the same value, so the team pays the same amount either way and has no reason to prefer one. The way to find it is to write the full cost of each plan as a function of the same input, such as the number of gigabytes stored, and set the two expressions equal. Solving that equation gives the input at which the plans match. The comparison is only meaningful if both rules are written for the same input over the same range, and if the ticket includes any one-time fees, they belong in the rule where they occur rather than being dropped.

questions.explanation: A break-even point is where two cost rules give the same value for one input. Each rule must be written completely, since a missing fee changes where the match happens.
questions.hint: Write both plans as functions of the same quantity.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Discount followed by a tax
questions.learningObjective: explain the order in which a discount and a tax must be applied
questions.stem: A software team's ticket lists a quoted price, a discount rate, and a tax rate. Explain what order the two rates should be applied in and why.

answer.exemplar: The discount should be applied first, because it reduces the amount the customer pays for the item, and the tax is then charged on that reduced amount. With a price of P, a 20 percent discount gives 0.80P, and an 8 percent tax on that gives 0.80P times 1.08. The two multipliers do not commute in general: swapping them would apply the discount to a price that already includes tax, and since a discount and a tax act on different bases, the final totals differ. The practical rule is that a discount always comes before any tax, because the tax is defined as a percentage of the sale price the customer actually pays.

questions.explanation: The discount comes first, because the tax is a percentage of the amount the customer pays after the discount. That is why the two multipliers are applied one after the other rather than added together.
questions.hint: The tax is charged on the discounted amount.

answer.exemplar: Age problems work best when one age is expressed in terms of the other, using a second equation to connect the two. If the older colleague is y years old, the younger is y minus 4, and the ticket says the older one is 2 times the younger, so the equation y = 2(y - 4) holds. Solving gives y = 8 for the older colleague, and checking shows 8 equals 2 times 4, which is true. Writing the relationship in terms of a single unknown keeps the equation to one line and makes the check at the end possible.

questions.explanation: Writing both ages in terms of one unknown, such as the older age, gives a single equation to solve. The two ages must also be linked by a second relationship, such as their fixed difference.

answer.exemplar: Converting a rate means changing the units of the input, and the size of the rate changes with them. A rate of 45 requests per minute measures how much happens in one minute, so in an hour, which is 60 minutes, the same service handles 45 times 60, which is 2700 requests. The requests do not change, only the window of time they are counted over, and the number must be relabeled as requests per hour. A common mistake is to report 2700 and still call it a per-minute rate, which would overstate the service by a factor of 60.

questions.explanation: An hour holds 60 minutes, so 45 requests each minute becomes 45 times 60, which is 2700 requests per hour. The count of requests stays the same, but the time window it is measured over changes.

options.misconception: applies the tax to the original price instead of the discounted one

options.text: 70.40 dollars, because the tax and the discount should both apply to 80 dollars
options.misconception: applies both percentage changes to the original price

options.text: 88.00 dollars, because the discount and tax cancel out at these rates
options.misconception: assumes a discount and a tax of similar size cancel

options.text: 64.80 dollars, because 80 times 0.75 is 60 and 60 times 1.08 is 64.80

questions.explanation: The 25 percent discount cuts 80 dollars to 60, and the 8 percent tax then gives 60 times 1.08, which is 64.80 dollars. Applying the tax to the original 80 would charge tax on money the customer never paid.
questions.hint: The tax follows the discount, not the other way around.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Age problem set as an equation
questions.learningObjective: solve for two ages that satisfy a multiple and a difference
questions.stem: A software team's ticket says one engineer is 6 years older than another engineer and 3 times as old as the intern, and the intern is 4 years old. What are the older and younger engineers' ages?

options.text: 12 years and 6 years, since the older engineer is 3 times 4 and 6 less gives the younger one
10 years and 4 years, since the older engineer is 4 plus 6 and the intern is 4
options.misconception: adds the age gap to the intern instead of using the multiple

options.text: 12 years and 18 years, since the 6 year gap is added to the intern's age instead
options.misconception: adds the age gap instead of subtracting it from the older age

options.text: 8 years and 2 years, since the older engineer is twice the intern plus the 6 year gap
options.misconception: uses two times the intern instead of the stated multiple

questions.explanation: The older engineer is 3 times the intern's 4 years, which is 12 years, and subtracting the 6 year gap gives the younger engineer at 6 years. Adding the gap would make the younger one older than the older one.
questions.hint: Find the older age first, then use the gap.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Rate with a unit conversion
questions.learningObjective: convert a travel time between seconds and minutes
questions.stem: A software team's ticket puts a conveyor at 0.5 meters per second to carry 90 meters. How many seconds does the trip take, and how many minutes is that?

options.text: 45 seconds, which is 0.75 minutes, because the rate is doubled to find the time
options.misconception: doubles the rate instead of dividing the distance by it

options.text: 180 seconds, which is 3 minutes, because 90 divided by 0.5 gives 180 seconds
180 seconds, which is 180 minutes, because the seconds label is kept after dividing
options.misconception: converts the seconds but leaves the minutes label unchanged

options.text: 90 seconds, which is 1.5 minutes, because the distance is divided by the distance
options.misconception: divides the distance by itself instead of by the rate

questions.explanation: Time equals distance divided by rate, so 90 meters at 0.5 meters per second takes 90 over 0.5, which is 180 seconds. Since a minute holds 60 seconds, that trip lasts 3 minutes.
questions.hint: Divide the distance by the rate, then convert the time.
